The main problem with binary voting systems is that there are two types of reasons why people vote up and down. Comments are voted up based on their relevancy or based on how popular/funny/agreeable they are. Trying to enforce any kind of ettiquite for voting is futile as long as there are no alternatives for people who silently disagree with a comment. The solution is simple:

Add another set of arrows next to all comments. This new set of arrows will be in two different colors and labeled** like-dislike**. The old set of arrows will be labeled relevant-irrelevant. Two arrows can be selected at a time for people who disagree with something but think it's still relevant to the discussion, or people who found a shitpost funny, but don't think it's appropriate for the thread.

By seperating relevancy and popularity, we give freedom for all kinds of users to tailor their vote experience to fit them. For non serious subs, I'd sort by populairty by default, while for more serious subs, I'd sort by relevancy.

I don't think it's possible to stop people from ragedownvoting or abusing the system if they are sufficiently determined, but we can give users the tools to seperate high effort posts from funny one liners without completely silencing one of the other.

My inspiration for this idea comes from Steams solution to people upvoting funny but totally unhelpful reviews about their games. Just by adding a "funny" button, they allowed good and informative reviews to float to the top, as funny ones were just marked as funny and stayed where they were. If a user wanted, he could check a box to hide "funny" but low scoring reviews. It worked really well for them, and I think it can work here.

More suggestions:

  • When one clicks the "irrelevant" button, add a small disableable popup to ask if the post is spam, and if it violates any subverse rules. This can help make people think twice before doing a "double downvote"

  • Ask users which type of comments they'd like to sort by default when subscribing to a new subverse

  • Allow users to autohide submissions that hit a negative threshold of downvotes for both votes.

  • clarify the language around the site. If we are to treat the current system like a ruler for relevancy and not just a like/dislike bar, then atko needs to scour this entire site of every instance of the word "like" used to describe voting. How can people upvote things they don't agree with when the site itself says "2 likes, 1 dislike"?

Short answer: Meh.

Long answer: Magic is okay occasionally, but it's not a game I would recommend "getting into." I have a few preconstructed decks laying around should the mood strike me to play it, but that's about it. The duel decks are fun because they're generally well balanced against each other, so the games then usually come down to play skills; and good times are had by both parties.

But, MTG hasn't aged particularly well compared to other card games that came after it (YuGiOh is a more well -designed game in my opinion, though I play it about as often as MTG). If you're willing to play competitively and deal with the fundamental flaws of the game, by all means do so. How ever many thousands or millions of people play it and are okay with the old, dilapidated mana system will gladly play. It's all subjective after all, and if I were to write a review of the game, I would say it's a mediocre game at best, even in its current state. But your opinion of the game may be vastly different than mine (as are many people's opinions of this game).

Really, all one can say is, try it, and if you like it, play it, but just go into it knowing it's far from the best-designed card game out there. If you're looking for silky, butter-smooth mechanisms and well-balanced cards, these aren't the droids you're looking for. If you're looking for a game where even the best player can and will lose games just because that's how MTG goes sometimes, then by all means, give it a whirl. Hell, give it a whirl regardless of its flaws, you may find you can look past them and enjoy it for what it is. It sure as shit ain't perfect, but it's a game a lot of people love, so there's something to it for sure.

 

Note: This is all in my personal opinion. No doubt many people will disagree with me, and that's fine. You keep on Untapping and drawing, and I'll keep on Rezzing and Running. It's all good.

I played MtG back in the original days (missed Beta unfortunately), through to around Urza's block. I probably sank $20-30k into cards/booster-boxes over that time. The game was (presumably still is) awesome. There is no other CCG that can even remotely compare IMO (I've tried designing a card game on a number of occasions and end up falling back on MtG mechanics). It is extraordinarily versatile (you can create dozens of viable decks, depending on what format you end up playing) and it is a game with epic strategy both in deck design and play. I look back on my days playing MtG with very fond memories.

That said, I tried to pick it up again a few years back and struggled to get back into it. It's a game with a lot of established history, so if you're coming into it new and you aren't just wanting to play the current block, it will take a lot of effort to familiarize yourself with every card. As you would have inferred, it is by no means a cheap hobby - if you have a large disposable income and no commitments, go for it, if not... let's just say it's addictive. If you have friends who play, they're not sinking a lot of money into it, and you're not intending to play tournaments, then I'd say go for it (you can still have a lot of fun for only a few hundred dollars).
